text:
Short answer: no. An all-women panel selecting a woman over you — another woman — isn't evidence of gender bias in any direction. The logic doesn't close. If anything, raising it would work against you: it would read as a reach, and it would make the organisation defensive at exactly the moment you want them talking openly about your candidacy. It can also leak into your reputation in what is probably a small professional community.

Panel composition would matter if there were a pattern — say, panels consistently drawn from one department that keeps selecting its own people, or a panel with no one qualified to assess technical depth for a technical leadership role. That second one might actually be worth a thought: was there anyone on that panel who could evaluate structural engineering judgement, or were they all from HR, operations, and client-facing roles? That's a real question about process design, and it has nothing to do with gender.

The line I'd actually focus on is "excellent client relationships."

That reads like the stated reason she got it. For a head-of-group role at a consultancy, that's not a tiebreaker — it's often the main job. Technical credibility gets you onto the shortlist; winning work, holding key accounts, and bringing in fee income gets you the chair. Fifteen years of design work and three major projects delivered demonstrate you can run the work. They don't by themselves demonstrate you can generate it, or that you can carry a P&L and a team's utilisation targets.

So the honest question to sit with is: in those two interviews, what did you say about business development, client retention, bidding, pricing, mentoring and managing underperformers? If you mostly talked about technical delivery and project leadership, you may have been answering for a different role than the one they were filling. Eight years is thin for that job on paper, which suggests she gave them something concrete on the commercial side that they valued more than your extra seven years of design.

On the unanswered request: two weeks of silence is poor practice but not unusual, and usually it's just inertia rather than stonewalling. Follow up once, in writing, keeping it brief and forward-looking — something like: you'd welcome a short conversation about development areas, as you intend to apply for similar roles and want to strengthen your candidacy. Framing it as development rather than justification makes it far more likely someone actually replies, because it doesn't sound like the opening move in a grievance.

Be aware that in most places there's no legal entitlement to written reasons for an unsuccessful external application. If this was an internal application, your employer's recruitment policy may give you more than that — worth checking. And if you want a candid answer, a verbal chat with one panel member is usually far more informative than anything that goes through HR in writing.
